contributions.headingText: Pineal parenchymal tumour of intermediate differentiation (PPTID) is a tumour of the pineal parenchyma that is intermediate in malignancy between pineocytoma and pineoblastoma, composed of diffuse sheets or large lobules of monomorphic round cells that appear more differentiated than those observed in pineoblastoma (CNS WHO grade 2 or 3).
9362/3 Pineal parenchymal tumour of intermediate differentiation
2A00.20 & XH1S48 Tumours of the pineal gland or pineal region & Pineal parenchymal tumour of intermediate differentiation
Not recommended: malignant pineocytoma; pineocytoma with anaplasia; pineoblastoma with lobules.

The clinical presentation is similar to that of other tumours of the pineal parenchyma (see under section Pineocytoma).

Imaging

PPTIDs usually appear larger and more heterogeneous than pineocytomas, and they often demonstrate local invasion {21080159}.

Spread

PPTIDs have the potential for local recurrence and craniospinal dissemination {10705018; 23396072; 24649332; 25911570}.

PPTIDs account for approximately 45% of all pineal parenchymal tumours {18808064; 23396072; 12075938; 21986148}. Median patient age is 33 years (range: 3.5–64 years). There is a slight female preponderance (M:F ratio: 0.8:1) {20418777; 23396072; 10668895; 12075938}.
No syndromic associations or genetic susceptibilities have been reported.

Cell of origin

The histogenesis of PPTID has been linked to the pinealocyte.

Genetic profile

Small in-frame insertions of KBTBD4 are recurrent and characteristic {30877433}. PPTIDs have relatively flat copy-number profiles, with some cases showing broad gains or losses {31768671; 11107183}.

On DNA methylation profiling, PPTID as a distinct molecular subgroup can be separated into two further subtypes: PPTID-A and PPTID-B {31768671}. The prognostic significance of these molecular subgroups requires further evaluation.
The macroscopic appearance is similar to that of pineocytomas.

PPTID may exhibit two architectural patterns: diffuse (neurocytoma- or oligodendroglioma-like) and/or lobulated (with vessels delineating vague lobules) {10668895}. PPTID is a potentially aggressive neoplasm and is characterized by moderate to high cellularity. The neoplastic cells usually harbour round nuclei showing mild to moderate atypia and salt-and-pepper chromatin. The cytoplasm of cells in PPTID is more easily distinguishable than in pineoblastoma.

Grading

The biological behaviour of PPTIDs is variable. Although the majority correspond to CNS WHO grade 2, more aggressive cases may correspond to grade 3, but definite histological grading criteria remain to be defined.

Proliferation

Mitotic activity is low to moderate {10668895}. The Ki-67 proliferation index ranges from 3.5% to 16.1% {18808064; 23396072; 11107183; 25911570; 21986148}.

Immunophenotype

PPTIDs usually stain positively for synaptophysin {18808064; 20418777; 23396072; 10668895}. Labelling for NFP and chromogranin A is variable {7839826; 10668895; 10746962; 12075938}. PPTIDs typically show diffuse (> 50% of cells) nuclear expression of CRX, a transcription factor involved in the differentiation of retinal and pineal lineages {28719464}.

Differential diagnosis

Histologically, PPTID may resemble central neurocytoma. Both have a sheet-like architecture, monomorphic round cells, and diffuse synaptophysin immunopositivity. However, PPTID does not express NeuN. Checking the imaging is critical, because a tumour in the pineal region resembling neurocytoma is most likely a primary pineal parenchymal tumour.

The histology of PPTID may also be confused with that of oligodendroglioma. PPTID does not express OLIG2 or show the typical molecular alterations of oligodendroglioma, such as IDH mutations and 1p/19q codeletion.

Mixed pineocytoma–pineoblastoma, composed of clearly delineated areas of pineoblastoma admixed with well-demarcated areas of pineocytoma {7821912; 8334641}, should not be diagnosed as PPTID (see section Pineoblastoma).

Although a morphological diagnosis is still acceptable in the absence of molecular data, evidence of a KBTBD4 alteration is considered highly desirable for the diagnosis of PPTID. The finding of this alteration in what appears to be another pineal parenchymal tumour type histologically, or conversely the absence of this alteration in a tumour otherwise resembling PPTID, should prompt careful consideration as to whether an alternative diagnosis may be more suitable.

In 29 studies including 127 patients with PPTID, median overall survival was 14 years, and the 5-year overall survival rate was 84% {27865543}. Median progression-free survival was 5.2 years, and the 5-year progression-free survival rate was 52% {27865543}; recurrences often involved spinal/leptomeningeal dissemination {27865543}.

In one study, low-grade PPTIDs were defined as tumours with a low mitotic count and expression of NFP in numerous cells {10668895}. In patients with low-grade PPTID, the 5-year overall survival rate was 74%. Recurrences occurred in 26% of patients and were mainly local and delayed {10705018}. High-grade PPTIDs were defined as tumours with a low mitotic count but no or only rare expression of NFP, or with a high mitotic count and NFP expression in numerous cells {10668895}. In patients with high-grade PPTID, the 5-year overall survival rate was 39%, and the risks of recurrence (56%) and spinal dissemination (28%) were higher than in patients with low-grade PPTID {10705018}. Low- and high-grade prognostic groups also showed different mean Ki-67 proliferation index values (5.2% vs 11.2%) {21696422}.

In another study, patients with low-grade PPTIDs (with a Ki-67 proliferation index of < 5%) had better overall survival and progression-free survival than did those with high-grade PPTIDs (with a Ki-67 proliferation index of ≥ 5%) {25911570}.

The prognostic role of mitotic count, NFP immunopositivity, and Ki-67 proliferation index requires confirmation by further studies, and the prognostic role of molecular subgrouping remains to be determined; consequently, there are currently no recommended grading criteria for PPTID.
